text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's Austrian newspapers:
DER STANDARD
- Austrian industry faces radical structural overhaul. Up to 80,000 jobs have been lost in the manufacturing sector from 1991 to 1994 alone.
- Austria's parliament votes to keep the age of consent for homosexuals unchanged at 18 years.
- Far-right leader Joerg Haider meets head of federal trade union congress Franz Verzetnitsch to outline his demands for radical structural change in the organisation.
- Consumer rights activists and Finance Minister Viktor Klima say they want to introduce laws to keep retailers from pushing up prices when Europe's single currency is introduced.
- Austrian companies' phone costs are 54 percent higher than those of their German counterparts.
- Austrian retailers are the most profitable companies in the country's economy.
- Strict savings at Austrian railways OeBB to result in pre-tax profit of about 300 million schillings this year.
- Leading bankers say low dividends and thin liquidity make Vienna's stock market unattractive for investors.
DIE PRESSE
- Pre-christmas shopping season may result in a loss for Austrian retailers as customers cut spending plans on the back of the government's austerity policy.
- OPEC ministers, meeting in Vienna, indicate they want to stick to current production quotas.
- Regional energy supplier EVN has upped its stake in national electricity grid Verbund to more than five percent.
- Construction group Bau Holding sees strong growth in profits for the full-year, bucking the industry's trend.
- Window maker Internorm to build a new plant worth 700 million schillings next year.

- New telecommunications company created jointly by railways OeBB and electricity grid Verbund plans to set up a new land-based phone network by 1998, but is still looking for an international partner.
KURIER
- Latest rumours in banking circles say Germany's Deutsche Bank or Dutch ING group may be interested in the state's stake in Creditanstalt.
WIRTSCHAFTSBLATT
- Bank Austria to create a 320 million schilling high-tech fund to invest in Austrian companies.
